newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria president warns of hardships ahead.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria president warns of hardships ahead.

text.p: Bulgarian president Petar Stoyanov on Wednesday warned the newly elected cabinet led by Prime Minister Ivan Kostov of hardships involved in hauling the country out of economic crisis.

"The new government has to win the war against poverty, the war against corruption, the war against crime, the war against inflation and the war for restoring the confidence and self-esteem of Bulgarians," Stoyanov told parliament.
With 179 votes in his favour, Kostov, leader of the reformist Union of Democratic Forces, was appointed by the 240 seat parliament as prime minister.
Speaking immediately after parliament appointed Kostov's cabinet, Stoyanov said Bulgaria's recovery and prosperity depended on the successful rule of the new cabinet.
"I will keep my fingers crossed throughout this cabinet's rule," said Stoyanov.

Among the new cabinet's first tasks will be the introduction in July of an IMF-prescribed currency board system, which is a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime designed to stabilise the country's shaky banks and volatile currency.
An IMF mission is now in Sofia to complete the preparations for the currency board.

Kostov will also be concentrating on passing this year's budget by July, closing loss-making state enterprises, speeding up privatisation and providing sufficient safety nets for those who are most effected by restructuring.
"Setting up a Foreign Investment Council and promoting investment opportunities in Bulgaria through road shows is also on the cabinet's agenda", said Kostov.
Stoyanov praised the previous cabinet for its legacy to the new government.

In its three-month rule the interim cabinet is credited with negotiating a $657 million accord with the International Monetary Fund which stabilised the national currency, bringing grain and fuel shortages under control and freeing prices and trade rules for most goods.
The lev has levelled to around 1,550 to the dollar from 3,000 in January and central bank foreign exchange reserves have grown to $1.250 billion in May.
Monthly inflation has plummeted to 0.7 percent in April from 243 percent in the crisis month of February, but year-on-year inflation remains at a galloping 1,965 percent.
